column5: sow wind; reap whirlwind; grain without yield
column6: Hosea makes wind sown into a whirlwind reaped, then says the stalk has no grain; it joins the commentary's storm, lost harvest, and failed human work in one agricultural judgment.

column5: rain drunk by earth; useful crop
column6: The earth repeatedly drinks rain and grows useful vegetation for its cultivators; this matches the commentary's rain-to-productive-growth sequence and makes the crop's value depend on what it yields.
The same watered earth bears thorns and ends in burning; this supplies a direct reversal of the commentary's fruitful growth destroyed at the end.
Ezekiel pictures a mother as a fruitful vine beside abundant water with many branches, paralleling the commentary's watered, connected vegetation as an image of a living group.

column5: east wind dries fruit; vine burned
column6: Ezekiel's once fruitful vine is uprooted, dried by the east wind, and consumed by fire; the reversal closely matches the commentary's lifetime yield destroyed by a fiery storm.
Fire emerging from the vine's own branch consumes its fruit and leaves no ruling branch; the commentary likewise reads the burned garden as a life's yield and vulnerable future lost together.
In Pharaoh's dream thin grain ears are scorched by the east wind; this gives the commentary's grain-ear stage a specific destructive counterpart before the harvest can feed anyone.
Seven thin ears consume the seven full ears in Pharaoh's dream; the image makes accumulated agricultural plenty disappear, as the commentary's late loss does.

column5: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; grain heaped
column6: Joseph orders grain from the good years to be heaped and guarded against famine; Hebrew צבר matches the commentary's secondary صبر image of piled food, though the table's sound match does not establish etymology.

column5: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; piled grain
column6: Joseph heaps grain in immense quantity before famine; the concrete stored-food heap corresponds to the commentary's صبرة of food stacked layer upon layer, without claiming proven cognacy.
Joseph says the collected food will preserve the land through seven famine years; this offers a deliberate preservation of yield against the harvest loss envisaged in the commentary.
The promised rains in their seasons allow Israel to gather grain, wine, and oil; this reproduces the commentary's move from rain cloud to usable produce.
God gives grass in the fields for livestock so that the people eat and are satisfied; it pairs the commentary's pasture feeding animals with the livelihood that follows.

column5: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; rain shut off
column6: The divine closing of the heavens stops rain and thus the land's produce; Hebrew עצר expresses restraint, a pointed reversal of the commentary's rain-releasing cloud and ensuing harvest.
The beloved prepares a vineyard and expects grapes but receives bad fruit; the text tests the commentary's claim that productive growth can figure the moral result of human work.
The vineyard's hedge is removed so it can be devoured and trampled; its protection gives way to destruction, as the commentary's flourishing garden does at the end.
God commands the clouds to give no rain to the now desolate vineyard; this reverses the commentary's rain-to-greenery sequence through judgment on a failed crop.
Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and the expected crop as justice and righteousness, clarifying how the commentary's harvest imagery can evaluate human conduct rather than farming alone.

column5: fire consumes crop for rejected law
column6: Fire consumes stubble and flame dries grass, while rotten roots and blown blossom picture those who rejected God's instruction; the commentary likewise lets a life crop end in fiery moral loss.
The people fail to acknowledge the giver of seasonal rain who preserves the appointed weeks of harvest; the verse makes rain and harvest an ordered provision with a moral obligation to recognize it.

column5: حق / חקק; table sound correspondence only; harvest ordinance
column6: Jeremiah's fixed harvest weeks use חקות from the table's חקק family; the prescribed season provides a concrete counterpart to the commentary's conjunction of the crop and its due right, without equating the words.
Jeremiah says sins have kept those good gifts from the people; the commentary's disappearance of yield likewise turns agricultural loss into a judgment on conduct.
The field's owner must leave the edge and gleanings at harvest; this gives an exact social practice beside the commentary's claim that a crop's right is given on harvest day.
Grapes and fallen fruit must be left for the poor and resident alien; the harvest right extends to the commentary's vineyard and makes fruitfulness support others.
A sheaf forgotten in the field is to remain for the foreigner, orphan, and widow; it specifies who receives the harvest's due, linking produce to the weak dependents in the commentary's garden scene.

column5: farmer waits for fruit and rains
column6: James urges patience by the farmer waiting for the precious crop and its early and late rains; the commentary's rain-grown yield is joined here to the explicit virtue of patient endurance.
Elijah prays again, heaven gives rain, and earth produces its fruit; this explicitly joins the commentary's rain cloud to its eventual productive crop in a communal prayer setting.
The withheld wages of harvest workers cry to the Lord in James's indictment of wealthy landowners; it gives the commentary's harvest due an economic and ethical edge.
Jesus describes good soil bearing fruit with perseverance after receiving the word; the commentary's patient, connected greenery becomes a specific figure for enduring faithful people.

column5: branch joined to vine bears fruit
column6: Jesus says a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine; this directly illuminates the commentary's unusual image of plants joined together as the condition of living growth.
The vine and branches produce much fruit through remaining joined; it supplies a relational image for the commentary's exception of people who sustain one another like contiguous plants.
A branch that does not remain is cast out, dries, is gathered, and burns; it states the exact contrary fate of the commentary's joined vegetation and burning garden.
Paul says a person reaps what he sows; the commentary's crop as the product of a life receives an explicit ethical harvest formula.
Sowing to the flesh yields corruption while sowing to the Spirit yields life; the two outcomes sharpen the commentary's distinction between a ruined yield and enduring good action.

column5: persist in good; harvest in time
column6: Paul urges against growing weary in doing good because a harvest will come if one does not give up; it ties the commentary's patient mutual goodness to sustained crop growth.
Jesus begins the rich fool's story with land yielding abundantly; this supplies the productive first stage of the commentary's lifetime crop lost near its end.
The man plans larger barns to store grain and goods; his amassed agricultural gain is the counterpart of the commentary's stacked food and accumulated life's produce.

column5: life ends before harvest can secure him
column6: God demands the man's life that night and asks who will own his stores; the reversal mirrors the commentary's late catastrophe that makes an accumulated yield useless.
Paul's giving appeal says sparing and generous sowing have corresponding harvests; this adds the commentary's almsgiving setting to its agricultural account of human gain.
In Paul's quotation, one who distributes to the poor has righteousness that endures; it explains how the commentary's crop right at harvest becomes a lasting moral yield.

column5: seed and bread; harvest of righteousness
column6: God supplies seed and food and multiplies the harvest of righteousness for givers; the commentary's rain-fed grain and obligation to share meet in this single farming image.
Bringing the tithe into God's storehouse is followed by promised abundance from heaven; it links the commentary's piled produce and due share with renewed provision.
God promises to restrain the devourer so field fruit is not destroyed and the vine does not fail; it reverses the commentary's loss of a ripened crop after its due has been given.
The righteous are a tree planted by channels of water that gives fruit in season; the commentary likewise sees the exceptional faithful as greenery sustained by water and productive time.
The wicked are chaff driven by wind, against the fruitful watered tree of the preceding verse; it precisely matches the commentary's contrast of lasting growth and works blown away.

column5: truth sprouts from earth beneath righteousness
column6: The psalm pictures truth springing from the earth while righteousness looks down from heaven; it gives the commentary's joined greenery and call to truth a striking common image.
The next verse promises the Lord's good gift and the land's yield; it supplies the harvest stage after truth springs from the ground in the preceding verse.

column5: fruit and green growth in old age
column6: The righteous still bear fruit in old age and remain fresh and green; this is an exact positive alternative to the commentary's aged owner losing a mature garden just when dependents need it.
Sowing in tears ends in reaping with joy; the agricultural sequence gives patient difficulty before harvest the positive ending preserved by the commentary's exception.

column5: sow without reaping; pressed crops lost
column6: Micah threatens that the people will sow but not reap, tread olives yet lack oil, and crush grapes yet not drink wine; this is the commentary's lost harvest in a judgment on unjust gain.
Haggai lists much seed with little harvest and wages disappearing as if through a pierced purse; it connects the commentary's failed crop to the vanishing gain of human labor.
The people bring home little of what they expected and God blows it away; the image matches the commentary's wind-scattered works and abrupt removal of accumulated yield.
Because of the people's neglect, heaven withholds dew and earth withholds its produce; the commentary's rain, growth, and loss are compressed into one reversal.
The called drought reaches grain, wine, oil, people, animals, and all labor of hands; it relates a failed harvest to the whole community and its work, as the commentary does.
Joel's devastated land has ruined fields and grain, alongside dried wine and failing oil; it gives a specific prophetic instance of the commentary's harvest as loss.
The vine and fig tree dry up, as do the other fruit trees, while human joy withers; it joins vegetative loss to lived human loss as in the commentary's ruined garden.
Joel cries to God because fire has devoured the wilderness pastures and burned trees; it gives the commentary's animal-feeding meadow a destructive fiery counterpart.
Joel promises early and later rain in restored measure; after the destroyed crop, this supplies a recovery of the commentary's rain-to-growth sequence.
The restored rains are followed by threshing floors filled with grain and vats with wine and oil; it gives a concrete positive answer to the commentary's lost and heaped harvest.
A person boasting of a gift never given is likened to clouds and wind without rain; this applies the commentary's rain cloud to its nearby warning about showy giving whose benefit vanishes.
Jesus warns against giving alms publicly for praise, because such givers have received their reward already; it directly illuminates the commentary's showy spending that yields no lasting benefit.

column5: poor person's crop swept away by injustice
column6: The poor person's field can provide much food, yet injustice destroys it; the verse makes the commentary's harvest right and lost yield a social issue rather than mere weather.

column5: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; withheld share causes lack
column6: The proverb says one who withholds what ought to be given comes to lack; Hebrew מחסור from חסר connects the commentary's lost gain with its duty to give a crop's share, while cognacy remains unverified.

column5: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; giver has no lack
column6: The one giving to the poor will have no lack, but ignoring them draws curses; Hebrew מחסור gives an explicit inverse to the commentary's loss and its harvest-day obligation.

column5: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; no lack
column6: The shepherd's speaker says he lacks nothing; Hebrew אחסר marks provision as the inverse of the commentary's ruined yield, and the following pasture image makes that inverse concrete.
The shepherd settles the speaker in green pastures beside quiet water; the commentary's meadow that gives itself to animals becomes a picture of sustained care.

column5: خسر / Aramaic חסר; table sound correspondence only; found deficient
column6: Daniel declares the king weighed and found lacking; the Aramaic חסיר gives the commentary's loss an explicitly evaluated human life, though the consonant match alone does not prove cognacy.

column5: حق / חקק; table sound correspondence only; rain prescribed
column6: God sets a prescribed order for rain; the Hebrew חק in a rain passage meets the commentary's rain sequence and its mention of a crop's due, while preserving the difference between ordinance and right.

column5: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; sky restrained
column6: Solomon describes heaven shut so there is no rain when Israel sins; עצר names the restraint, contrasting with the commentary's cloud releasing water onto a community.

column5: عصر / עצר; table sound correspondence only; closed sky and eaten land
column6: God says he can shut heaven against rain or send locusts to devour land; עצר makes a concrete opposite to the commentary's pressed rain cloud and fruitful harvest.
If God's people turn and pray, he promises to heal their land; this adds a communal ethical remedy to the preceding rain-and-crop destruction and the commentary's collective exception.

column5: mass of waters in thick clouds; חשר table sound match has different sense
column6: David's hymn depicts God surrounded by dense water clouds; it supports the commentary's layered, water-filled cloud image on its own terms, while the table's חשר is semantically distinct from Arabic خسر 'loss'.
God binds water within thick clouds without their bursting; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's cloud filled with rain before releasing it.
Job says the skies pour their drops abundantly upon humanity; the rain-laden cloud's release corresponds to the commentary's cloud giving water to a community.

column5: full cloud empties rain on land
column6: A cloud filled with water pours itself onto earth; this expresses the commentary's compressed rain cloud and its release without requiring a shared root.

column5: God gives rain and field plants
column6: Those asking for spring rain receive showers and field plants; the verse carries the commentary's paired images of rain cloud and resulting greenery.
Before the garden's plants had appeared, God had not yet caused rain on the earth; the negation makes rain the missing beginning of the commentary's sequence of growth.

column5: vine fruit, land produce, heavenly dew
column6: Zechariah's restored remnant receives a seed of peace, fruitful vine, productive ground, and heavenly dew; this unites the commentary's collective, watered garden, and tangible harvest.

column5: truth spoken to neighbors after restored harvest
column6: After promising dew and yield to the remnant, Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and judge justly; this connects the commentary's green community to its mutual exhortation in truth.
God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on hills; this gives the commentary's cloud-to-pasture transition in one verse.
The next verse says God gives food to animals; it connects the commentary's pasture given to herds to divine provision rather than vegetation alone.

column5: whirlwind and storm; clouds as dust
column6: Nahum joins a divine whirlwind and tempest with clouds described as dust beneath God's feet; this puts the commentary's rain cloud and dust-raising whirlwind into one memorable storm image.

column5: rain makes earth sprout, seed and bread
column6: Rain and snow water the earth so it sprouts and gives seed and bread; the commentary's cloud, joined growth, grain, and food yield follow this same ordered sequence.

column5: water on dry land and descendants
column6: God promises to pour water on thirsty ground and blessing on descendants; the commentary's rain-fed greenery and concern for weak offspring meet through this joined promise.
Those descendants sprout like grass among watercourses; the verse makes a living group into adjacent flourishing plants, as the commentary does for the mutually supporting faithful.
An outpouring from above transforms wilderness into a fruitful field; it gives the commentary's rain-to-garden movement a communal renewal sense.
Justice comes to dwell in the transformed fruitful field; the commentary likewise places truth and a crop's due amid flourishing vegetation.

column5: human generations swept away like grass
column6: The psalm says God sweeps people away as grass renewing in the morning; it places the commentary's human loss inside the short life cycle of vegetation.
Grass blossoms in the morning and withers by evening; it closely parallels the commentary's quick turn from luxuriant growth to destroyed yield.
The psalm reckons a human span as seventy or eighty years, full of trouble and swiftly gone; it adds the late-life horizon of the commentary's elderly garden owner to the nearby grass image.
James compares the rich person's passing to a wild flower; it joins the commentary's accumulated material yield with the brief life of vegetation.
A rising sun with scorching heat dries the grass and drops its flower, as the wealthy fade amid their pursuits; this is another sudden destruction of apparent prosperity.
The letter quotes human flesh as grass whose flower falls; it transposes the commentary's withering harvest to the brevity of human life.

column5: blade then ear then full grain
column6: Jesus describes the earth producing first a blade, then an ear, then full grain in the ear; the commentary's distinctive attention to visible grain husks and mature crop finds a staged analogue.
When the grain is ripe, the sower sends the sickle because harvest has come; it provides the decisive harvest moment beside the commentary's produce and harvest-day obligation.
In Jesus' explanation, wealth's deceit chokes the word so it becomes unfruitful; it offers an ethical counterpart to the commentary's showy spending and lost crop.
The receptive person is good soil that bears a multiplied crop; the commentary's exceptional believers likewise appear as productive ground after the warning of loss.

column5: seed on bare rock withers for lack of moisture
column6: Seed on rock sprouts but dries because it has no moisture; the commentary's hard bare stone is a precise contrary surface to its watered, continuous greenery.

column5: rain and wind test true work
column6: Rain, floods, and winds strike the house that survives because its builder acted on Jesus' words; this gives the commentary's storm a test of lived conduct rather than a mere weather event.

column5: rain and wind destroy failed work
column6: The same storm makes the house of the hearer who does not act collapse; it parallels the commentary's image of a whole life's work lost in a violent final event.

column5: planting and watering; growth from God
column6: Paul assigns planting and watering to different workers while God causes growth; the commentary's rain-fed community of mutually contributing lives receives a concrete division of work.

column5: fire reveals quality of each work
column6: Paul says the day exposes each person's work as fire tests its quality; it links the commentary's burning at the end to an evaluation of accumulated human work.
If a person's work burns, that person suffers loss even though saved; the precise distinction between a life and its ruined product clarifies the commentary's garden consumed late in life.

column5: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; piled wealth
column6: The wicked man may heap silver like dust, yet the following verse gives it to others; צבר matches the commentary's piled store while the context makes accumulation vulnerable to loss.

column5: صبر / צבר; table sound correspondence only; life's hoard
column6: The passing human heaps up wealth without knowing who will gather it; צבר joins the commentary's stacked gain to the old-age question of what a life's product finally secures.
The transplanted vine is set in good soil beside abundant water so it can bear branches and fruit; it parallels the commentary's rain-fed connected plants that grow into yield.
Even a planted vine will wither when the east wind touches it; the commentary's productive garden similarly remains vulnerable to a destructive wind.

column5: wind kills children at life's height
column6: A great wind strikes the house where Job's children are together and kills them; it offers a family-loss counterpart to the commentary's storm scene with vulnerable offspring, though Job's loss is not a garden fire.

column5: east wind carries away accumulated wealth
column6: The east wind drives away the wicked person after the account of his piled silver; the commentary likewise makes wind undo accumulated gain.
Job asks whether the wicked become chaff before wind and straw snatched by a whirlwind; the wording puts a human fate in the commentary's image of works scattered by a violent wind.
The nations' tumult is rebuked and chased like mountain chaff before wind and rolling dust before a storm; this shares the commentary's dust-raising whirlwind as an image of works unable to remain.
After the flood, God promises seedtime and harvest will continue while the earth remains; this stable cycle sets the ordinary expectation against which the commentary's ruined harvest is a reversal.
The generous person prospers and the one who gives water receives water; the commentary's rain-fed, mutually joined plants become an ethical pattern of reciprocal support.
Measured manna leaves neither surplus for the great gatherer nor lack for the small one; it offers an alternative to the commentary's stacked private food by meeting each person's need.

column5: خسر / חסר; table sound correspondence only; no food deficit
column6: The smaller manna gatherer does not lack, using חסר; the negated deficiency connects the commentary's loss to a shared-food scene that prevents it.
Paul asks that one community's present abundance supply another's need; this makes the commentary's mutually joined believers and harvest due a concrete exchange of resources.

column5: consider one another for good works
column6: The community is to attend to one another so as to stir love and good works; this gives a specific ethical action beside the commentary's joined plants representing believers who mutually urge what is right.
Those who fear the Lord speak with one another and are heard and remembered; their reciprocal speech provides a human counterpart to the commentary's plants joining in a faithful group.
Birds neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, yet God feeds them; the commentary's stores of grain and pasture for animals meet a different account of secure provision.
Grass now growing in the field is soon thrown into an oven; the commentary's green abundance suddenly consumed by fire gains a short-lived plant counterpart.

At harvest the weeds are bundled for burning while wheat is gathered into a barn; this places the commentary's stored grain and final fire at one decisive sorting, though its garden fire acts on an already productive plot.

column5: last season to make fig tree fruitful
column6: The gardener asks for one more year to tend the fruitless fig tree; this creates a patient interval before the kind of final crop judgment the commentary describes.
If the tree bears after tending it may remain, otherwise it will be cut down; the commentary's survival of fruitful growth and loss of an unproductive garden meet in this conditional ending.

God withholds rain from one city while another receives it, leaving one field watered and another dry; the commentary's cloud releasing rain upon a group becomes an ethical question of who receives it.
God strikes gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees with blight and insects; this provides a more gradual counterpart to the commentary's storm destroying a developed crop.
Grass dries and flowers fall when God's breath blows on them; the commentary's wind-driven loss of lush vegetation likewise turns growth into impermanence.

Isaiah pairs whirlwind and tempest with the flame of a devouring fire in a judgment scene; it is a specific storm-and-fire analogue to the commentary's fiery whirlwind, though no crop is named in this verse.

Jeremiah calls prosperous people fat and sleek while they fail to defend an orphan's claim; it turns the commentary's image of fattening from abundant food toward the obligation to support vulnerable people.
Honi asks first for rain, then for rain of favor when the downpour is too violent; the story distinguishes life-giving rain from a damaging storm within the commentary's weather sequence.

A man brings firstfruits and fresh grain ears to Elisha, who orders them given to the people; the commentary's ears becoming food and a due share can be read beside this concrete communal distribution.

column5: field corner and firstfruits as obligations
column6: The Mishnah lists the field corner and firstfruits among duties with no fixed measure; it gives a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's claim that a crop carries a right owed to others at harvest.

Job describes a thick cloud burdened with moisture while its luminous cloud disperses; the burdened cloud resembles the commentary's rain-filled layers, but its release into a community is not explicit here.
God promises rains in season and land yielding produce for obedience; the sequence is exact, though it does not include the commentary's mutual plant growth or later violent loss.
The coming figure gathers wheat into the barn and burns chaff; it juxtaposes stored harvest with final fire, though the commentary's fire consumes a whole garden rather than separated chaff.
